opus-5.5.text:
I think the useful way to think about it is less "which tasks" and more "how much context does the task require, and how well can you check the answer."

At one end, you have work that's well-specified and verifiable: fix this failing test, migrate this codebase from one library version to another, write a function that meets this spec. The agent can try something, run it, see if it works, and iterate. That loop is exactly what these models are getting very good at, and I think that end of the spectrum is going to be largely automated, and fairly soon.

At the other end, you have work where the hard part isn't writing code at all. It's figuring out what should be built. Talking to the customer, understanding why the system was designed the way it was five years ago, making a judgment call about which trade-off matters for the business. A lot of senior engineering is really that: holding a huge amount of implicit context in your head and making decisions under ambiguity. Agents struggle there, not because they can't reason, but because the context often isn't written down anywhere they can access, and there's no clean signal telling them whether they got it right.

So in the near term, I think the programmer's job shifts. You spend less time typing code and more time acting as a manager of agents: breaking the problem down, specifying what you want, reviewing the output, and deciding what "done" means. The skill that becomes most valuable is taste and judgment about the problem, not fluency in the syntax.

Over time, that boundary moves. As models get longer context, better memory, and more ability to go gather information themselves, more of that ambiguous work comes within reach. But I'd expect the last thing to go is the part where someone has to decide what we actually want, because that's ultimately a human question.

r001.rationale: It says well-specified, verifiable work suits agents and gives examples where they can run the result, check it, and iterate.

r002.rationale: It mentions taste and judgment as valuable, but does not identify the degree of implementation taste required as the boundary between agent-suitable work and work requiring human programmers.

r003.rationale: It discusses longer context and memory over time, but does not ask whether detailed specifications or architecture diagrams could let agents continue across context-window boundaries.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the line keeps moving, and it moves in a pretty predictable direction. The way I'd frame it is: the agent is good at anything where you can specify the task clearly and verify the result. If I can say "make this test pass" or "add this endpoint that behaves like these other three endpoints," and there's a way to check that it actually worked, an agent can take that end to end today. Not perfectly, but well enough that you'd rather review its pull request than write the thing yourself.

Where it gets hard is the part that happens before the specification exists. Someone has to decide what we're building and why, what the right abstraction is, which of the five ways to structure this is going to still make sense in a year. That's judgment, and it's judgment that depends on context the model mostly doesn't have: what the customers are complaining about, what the team can maintain, what the organization is actually trying to do. I don't think that's a permanent limitation, but it's the part that's clearly still human right now.

The interesting thing is that the middle of the spectrum is where most of the real change is happening. A lot of engineering work isn't pure specification and isn't pure execution. It's reading an unfamiliar codebase, figuring out why something's broken, deciding whether to fix it properly or patch it. A year or two ago the agents were pretty useless there. Now they can do a lot of the investigation, and the human's role shifts to being the one who sets the direction and checks the reasoning rather than the one typing.

So I'd say the spectrum isn't really "easy tasks for agents, hard tasks for people." It's more like time horizons and taste. The agents handle longer and longer chunks of work, and humans keep getting pushed up toward the question of what's worth doing in the first place. If you're a programmer, the skill that's appreciating is the ability to decompose a goal into things you can verify, and then to recognize when the result is wrong even though it looks right. That last one, by the way, is the thing I'd worry about most. The failure mode isn't the agent that can't do the task. It's the agent that does it confidently and slightly wrong, and nobody in the loop knows enough to notice.

r001.rationale: It says agents can handle tasks that are clearly specified and have a way to verify that they worked.

r002.rationale: It mentions taste and human judgment about abstractions, but does not clearly identify the degree of implementation taste required as a boundary for current agent capability.

r003.rationale: It does not ask whether detailed specifications or architecture diagrams could sustain progress across context-window boundaries.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a spectrum, and a lot of it comes down to how well you can specify the task and how easily you can check the result. If you can say, “Here’s a bug, here’s how to reproduce it, and here’s what should happen,” that’s a pretty good task for an autonomous agent. It can work through the code, make a change, run tests, and iterate.

At the other end, you might say, “We need to make this product better.” The hard part there isn’t necessarily writing the code. It’s figuring out what users need, deciding which tradeoffs to make, and understanding constraints that nobody has written down. That requires much more human judgment and interaction.

And there’s a lot in between. A programmer might figure out the approach, delegate pieces to agents, and then review how those pieces fit together. So I don’t think the boundary is simply easy code versus hard code. A technically difficult task can be very delegable if the goal is clear and you have a reliable way to evaluate it. A small change can require a human if it depends on knowing what the business actually wants.

r001.rationale: It says tasks are good for agents when the goal is clear and the result is easy to check, giving a reproducible bug and expected behavior as an example.

r002.rationale: It discusses human judgment, tradeoffs, and unstated constraints, but does not identify the degree of implementation taste required as the boundary.

r003.rationale: It does not ask whether detailed specifications or architecture diagrams could help agents continue across context-window boundaries.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as a spectrum of how well you can specify the task and how easily you can check whether it’s done. If you have a well-defined bug, a way to reproduce it, and tests that tell you whether you fixed it, that’s a great task for an agent. You can let it work fairly independently and then review the result.

At the other end, you have something like, “What should we build for our customers?” That involves understanding people, making tradeoffs, and deciding what success even means. A human programmer is often doing all of those things alongside writing code.

And there’s a lot in between. You might know the feature you want, but there are architectural decisions or ambiguous requirements. The agent can do substantial work, then come back to a person at those decision points. So I don’t think the division is simply agents writing easy code and humans writing hard code. It’s also about how much context and judgment the task requires, and whether you can give the agent a useful feedback loop.

r001.rationale: It says agents are well suited to well-defined bugs with reproducible cases and tests that verify the fix.

r002.rationale: It mentions architecture decisions, tradeoffs, and judgment, but does not identify the degree of implementation taste required as the boundary.

r003.rationale: It does not ask whether detailed specifications or architecture diagrams could let agents continue across context-window boundaries.
